title: Optimal Design of Toll Plaza Based on Minimum Risk Maximum Flow

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical page 1 is the summary sheet, pages 2-3 are contents, and physical pages 4-28 carry printed Pages 1-25 of 26; the printed counter does not imply a missing physical page.

notes: All 28 physical pages were read completely in page-bounded text ranges, including summary, both contents pages, every substantive section, conclusion, strengths/weaknesses, future improvements, authority letter, references, service-level annexes, capacity matrix, and code.

Four seven-page JPEG contacts and four focused JPEG crops totaled 2,295,566 bytes; the largest was 444,811 bytes, each image call returned one image, and no original full-page PNG entered model transport.
Focused review reconciled Equations (3)-(7), (21)-(22), (24)-(25), and the Annex 3 capacity matrix; all 28 original PNGs remain local coordinate authority.
No blank, black, clipped, overlapping, missing, or failed-render page was found; physical page 3 is an intentionally sparse contents continuation.

context_sources: The paper cites toll-plaza planning, capacity, delay, traffic conflict, microsimulation, tollbooth traffic flow, and variable-speed-control literature.

No official prompt, raw AADT/time-series/service data, risk-curve dataset, complete graph ledger, field geometry, crash/conflict observations, LINGO project, MATLAB source package, solver output, or uncertainty ledger is bundled with the PDF.

inputs: booth service/departure behavior and service level
outputs: New Jersey design and authority recommendation
decisions: how many toll lanes to build or operate
how booth traffic should merge into main lanes
how much fan-in/fan-out land is required
how design changes with demand and technology
what evidence is needed before deployment

section_map.summary: Input: A toll-plaza design must trade accident exposure, traffic flow, and construction footprint while specifying geometry and merging. Rhetorical job: Preview the three-stage model chain, its scenario tests, the New Jersey application, and the authority-facing deliverable in execution order. Analytical job: Attach every headline number to the model or scenario that produces it, keeping lane count, merge flow, accident rate, area, autonomy, and booth mix distinct. Output: A complete decision preview: seven one-way toll lanes in the baseline, a 1375 veh/h route branch, a reported 0.9-0.96% accident rate, a 4650.1875 m2 plaza, and a ten-lane New Jersey case. Handoff: The introduction explains the public-road mechanism, research gap, and four work packages behind the preview.

Input: Expressway growth makes toll plazas a localized bottleneck where service demand, queueing, fan-in, and unsafe lane changes interact. Rhetorical job: Move from broad transport importance to the toll-plaza failure mechanism, then review capacity and safety studies before stating the synthesis gap and work map. Analytical job: Separate cited background, observed mechanism, literature coverage, unresolved design gap, and the paper's own analytical commitments. Output: A four-part agenda covering toll-lane count, risk-flow merging, minimum-area geometry, and performance under traffic, autonomy, and booth-composition changes. Handoff: The overall/key-point analysis converts that agenda into three decision tensions and a scoped assumption ledger.

section_map.section: 2 Analysis of Overall and Key Points
section_map.summary: Input: The toll-plaza design must carry vehicles safely from L highway lanes through B service lanes and back while controlling congestion, conflict, and land cost. Rhetorical job: Restate the goal through three key-point subsections so each later model has one visible decision job. Analytical job: Map lane count to demand/service, merging to throughput/safety, and size to following/braking distance and cost. Output: Three typed problem interfaces with distinct inputs, criteria, and downstream models. Handoff: The assumptions and symbol table bound the interfaces before equations are introduced.

Input: A tractable toll-plaza model requires vehicle classes, speed behavior, roadway condition, directional symmetry, and booth orientation to be fixed. Rhetorical job: Pair every assumption with a stated reason so simplification remains inspectable rather than implicit. Analytical job: Distinguish fleet aggregation, kinematic uniformity, geometric symmetry, and orientation constraints because they fail in different ways. Output: A conditional domain for the queue, network-flow, and area models. Handoff: The notation and overall flow chart expose which variables consume these premises.

Input: The three model layers exchange demand, capacity, lane count, risk, distance, time, and queue quantities. Rhetorical job: Provide a compact symbol table and a workflow figure before detailed derivations. Analytical job: Keep similar-looking symbols such as N/B, M/c_ij, T_q/T_d, and S'/D' attached to their model roles and units. Output: A typed interface from toll-lane determination through merging and area sizing to parameter checks and the New Jersey case. Handoff: Model I begins by selecting a reasonable number of toll lanes.

Input: A toll plaza becomes a bottleneck when design-hour demand exceeds capacity at the chosen service level. Rhetorical job: Introduce lane-count logic from qualitative factors, then quantify design-hour volume and single-lane service capacity. Analytical job: Separate forecast demand, charging/service time, and service-level choice before solving for lane count. Output: DHV and single-lane capacity M as inputs to the multi-lane queue model. Handoff: The M/G/K section computes stay, delay, and queue length for candidate N.

Input: Candidate lane counts must be evaluated under stochastic service and departure time rather than by single-lane capacity multiplication alone. Rhetorical job: Move from expected service/departure moments through queue wait, total stay, queue length, and vehicle delay. Analytical job: Retain each moment, summation limit, lane-count exponent, and stability denominator because small notation changes alter the queue model. Output: T_q, T_d, L_q, and d for each candidate N and arrival intensity lambda. Handoff: Service-level thresholds translate these outputs into a lane-selection rule.

Input: Queue length and delay must be converted into a service-level criterion and a traffic-intensity lookup for candidate lane counts. Rhetorical job: Explain qualitative level bands, present the intensity table, and derive the hourly throughput inequality before selecting N. Analytical job: Keep q/s, n_N, service time S, DHV, and the table lookup in one auditable chain. Output: A minimum candidate N satisfying the required service level and N' > DHV. Handoff: The worked New Jersey baseline reports seven one-way toll lanes and then tests DHV sensitivity.

Input: The symbolic lane rule must be instantiated and its response to traffic demand checked. Rhetorical job: Give an algebraic four-step algorithm, report the baseline inputs/result, then vary demand and interpret the plotted staircase. Analytical job: Separate assumed service level and service time from observed or queried traffic volume and from the resulting lane count. Output: A seven-lane one-way baseline and a positive, discrete relationship between hourly traffic and required lanes. Handoff: Model II consumes the selected B while optimizing the merging network.

Input: Given L main lanes and B toll lanes, post-service vehicles need an explicit network allocation that balances throughput and accident exposure. Rhetorical job: Abstract input, booths, arcs, and merge point into G=(V,A,C), define risk from volume/capacity ratio, combine objectives, and state flow/capacity constraints. Analytical job: Retain the distinction between arc flow H_ij, capacity c_ij/M_ij, accident rate b_ij, net flow v, demand d_i, and penalty lambda. Output: A constrained objective max E = v - lambda sum b_ij H_ij with node balances and arc capacities. Handoff: The labeling algorithm searches augmenting paths and the worked network assigns flows across 22 intermediate nodes.

Input: The risk-flow formulation requires a constructive maximum-flow route and a toll-lane capacity instantiation. Rhetorical job: Explain labeling and flow adjustment step by step, then map charging modes and capacities to a numbered network, route table, and merge diagram. Analytical job: Separate the generic augmenting-path algorithm, LINGO implementation, capacity inputs, selected paths, and reported aggregate accident rate. Output: A 3000 veh/h five-toll-lane example with route groups carrying 1375, 976, and 649 veh/h and reported total accident rate 0.96%. Handoff: Model III uses the resulting operation and kinematics to size a symmetric plaza.

Input: Land and road costs require the acceleration/deceleration footprint to be minimized while maintaining following and braking distances. Rhetorical job: Move from location principles and stable-flow assumptions to rear-car braking, two-car safety distance, a weighted objective, numerical length, and final area. Analytical job: Keep v1/v2, a1/a2, reaction time, braking deceleration, S0, S', D', weights, symmetry, and the geometric area calculation distinct. Output: A symmetric 65.25 m acceleration/deceleration length and reported area 4650.1875 m2. Handoff: The testing section perturbs traffic, autonomy, and booth mix around the selected design.

Input: A single baseline design needs performance checks under changed demand, autonomous-vehicle inflow, and tollbooth technology proportions. Rhetorical job: Use one-factor-at-a-time scenario branches with tables and diagrams, reporting how flow, accident rate, length, lane mix, and footprint respond. Analytical job: Keep each perturbation's fixed parameters, changed input, recalculated output, comparator, and evidence boundary visible. Output: Traffic-flow saturation at 3000 veh/h, an added 500 autonomous vehicles, and a 3:1:1 booth mix with 57.31 m acceleration length. Handoff: The New Jersey case combines the model layers with site-specific inputs.

Input: The general models must be instantiated for a named New Jersey highway with traffic, lane, booth, width, and acceleration/deceleration inputs. Rhetorical job: Collect site parameters, analyze daily flow, relax equal acceleration/deceleration, compute the design, and compare it with the existing scheme. Analytical job: Separate queried site data, chart-derived flow, maintained-length assumptions, MATLAB output, diagram geometry, and comparative claims. Output: Ten toll lanes in a 5:3:2 mix, a reported 9614.5-9614.56 m2 area, and a 44.8 degree/131 m fan geometry. Handoff: The conclusion synthesizes the three models and scenario evidence before strengths and limitations.

Input: The completed chain contains lane sizing, network merging, footprint geometry, scenario tests, and a New Jersey application. Rhetorical job: Revisit the models in the same order as the work map and repeat the principal directional findings without introducing new methods. Analytical job: Distinguish computed lane/area outputs from qualitative claims about accident rate, autonomy, and booth proportions. Output: A bounded synthesis that points from demand and service to lanes, from flow/capacity to risk, and from braking/following to area. Handoff: The next section explicitly records strengths, weaknesses, and future improvements.

Input: The modeling chain contains useful abstractions but depends on symmetry, homogeneous units, fixed distributions, and planar geometry. Rhetorical job: Separate positive reusable choices from admitted limitations, then map each weakness to a concrete future extension. Analytical job: Do not let robustness language substitute for parameter provenance, distribution tests, heterogeneous service, or field validation. Output: A repair agenda covering stochastic flow, asymmetric geometry, heterogeneous booths, and a possible multi-level plaza. Handoff: The authority letter translates the technical chain and caveats into audience-facing advice.

section_map.section: 11 Letter to the New Jersey Highway Authority
section_map.summary: Input: A public authority needs a concise design rationale, site-specific outputs, and explicit deployment caveats rather than the full derivation alone. Rhetorical job: Mirror the three technical models in plain decision order, then summarize scenario behavior and the New Jersey design table. Analytical job: Keep technical evidence, recommendation, ideal-condition limitation, and authority responsibility in separate clauses. Output: An advisory sequence for lane count, merging pattern, plaza size, operating scenarios, and a ten-lane 5:3:2 case. Handoff: References and appendices preserve source provenance, service classifications, matrices, and code.

Input: The model relies on external transport sources, qualitative service levels, an arc-capacity matrix, and LINGO/MATLAB implementations. Rhetorical job: Preserve provenance and executable-looking detail after the argument, while distinguishing what is printed from what can actually be reproduced. Analytical job: Track citation scope, table meaning, matrix dimensions, code objective, data vectors, and absent software/version/run outputs. Output: A provenance tail containing 15 references, two service-level tables, the capacity matrix, two LINGO programs, and one MATLAB calculation. Handoff: The staging artifacts retain every physical page, formula, visual, and implementation boundary.

assumptions.summary: Vehicles are grouped as large, medium, and small using charging and physical characteristics.
Two-way traffic is symmetric, allowing one-way analysis to represent both directions.
Vehicles of the same class share a speed within the studied region.
Road surface, alignment, sight distance, and weather are treated as favorable and outside the design variation.
Vehicle input and merging areas are geometrically symmetric.
Tollbooths are perpendicular to the lane entry so vehicles enter smoothly and delay is reduced.
Normal traffic consists of standard small cars at minimum headway with no directional interference.
When booth service can accept demand, drivers freely choose payment methods without congestion.
Service and departure times follow normal distributions and their variances add.
A selected q/s band and Table 2 adequately encode the desired service level.
Peak traffic is the relevant regime for the merging model.
Arc accident rate is represented by a cited quadratic in traffic-volume/capacity ratio.
Input, toll, and merge regions can be represented by a directed capacity graph.
Same-lane same-direction vehicles form a stable flow with a meaningful safety spacing.
Base acceleration and deceleration regions are symmetric and share length 65.25 m.
Traffic-flow testing changes only demand while all other parameters remain fixed.
Autonomous vehicles use only automatic toll lanes and take the inner lane.
The New Jersey case holds total plaza length fixed while acceleration and deceleration differ.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The design-hour factors are K=0.12 and D=0.60, with D's stated range 0.55-0.65.
Single-lane capacity is 3600 divided by standard service plus departure time.
Table 2 gives traffic-intensity values for N=1-8 and q/s=0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0.
The worked lane calculation states AADT=38594, q/s=1.5, K=0.12, service time 6 s, DHV=4578, intensity=0.7716, and seven toll lanes.
The accident curve uses coefficients 6.2343, -7.2219, and 2.7091.
The merge example uses demand 3000 veh/h, three main lanes, and five toll lanes.
Automatic, semi-automatic, and labor lanes are listed at capacities 727, 703, and 624 veh/h.
The booth order is two automatic, two semi-automatic, and one manual from inside to outside.
Table 5 groups route flows as 1375, 976, and 649 veh/h with total accident rate 0.96 percent.
The kinematic query reports friction coefficient 0.75, reaction time 0.6 s, and acceleration 7.39 m/s2.
MATLAB reports a 65.25 m acceleration length; symmetry assigns the same deceleration length.
Figure 6 uses 50 m toll width, 22.5 m main width, 48 m booth length, and 65.25 m fans.
The base plaza area is reported as 4650.1875 m2.
Table 6 varies traffic from 1500 to 4250 veh/h in 250-vehicle increments and prints accident rates from 0.91 to 0.963 percent.
The maximum-flow curve is described as saturating at 3000 veh/h.
The autonomy scenario adds 500 vehicles and prints route groups 1476, 1065, and 826 veh/h.
Table 7 reports 0.96 percent total accident rate and Figure 9 shows 62.25 m.
The booth-mix scenario changes automatic:semi-automatic:manual from 2:2:1 to 3:1:1 and acceleration length from 65.25 to 57.31 m.
Table 9 prints four main lanes, 14 m lane width, 12 existing toll lanes, and 70 m deceleration area.
The New Jersey daily chart is interpreted as peaking near 07:00 at 106 veh/min, reaching 15 veh/min minimum, and averaging 2634 veh/h.
Table 10 reports 10 toll lanes, a 5:3:2 mix, and area 9614.5 m2.
Figure 12 prints a 44.8 degree fan angle, 131 m length, and 26 m width label.
Fifteen references support general toll design, capacity, delay, safety, simulation, and traffic-flow context.
Annex 3 and the LINGO capacity vector preserve sparse arc capacities including zero and infinite entries.

models.summary: Translate forecast demand and charging time into the two inputs needed for multi-lane lane sizing.
Map service/departure moments and candidate lane counts to waiting time, stay, queue length, delay, and service-level bands.
Select the minimum toll-lane count satisfying a chosen service level, then vary demand to inspect the discrete response.
Allocate post-toll traffic over a directed capacity network while trading net throughput against an exposure-weighted risk surrogate.
Find augmenting paths, instantiate a 24-node graph, and report a 3000 veh/h five-booth merge pattern with route-group flows.
Use rear braking and two-vehicle safety distances to set a symmetric acceleration/deceleration length and plaza area.
Vary input traffic from 1500 to 4250 veh/h and compare reported accident rate and the 3000 veh/h maximum-flow ceiling.
Add 500 autonomous vehicles and change the booth mix to 3:1:1, then report route flows, acceleration length, lane needs, and capacity direction.
Apply the lane, merge, and geometry chain to a New Jersey data table and daily flow chart with unequal acceleration/deceleration assumptions.
Retain service-level classifications, the arc-capacity matrix, LINGO listings, and MATLAB vectors while distinguishing printed code from reproducible execution.

Directional design-hour demand enters the lane feasibility inequality directly.

Demand and road capacities provide flow and volume-capacity inputs to the risk curve.
The capacitated risk-flow program is instantiated by the labeling algorithm and LINGO network.
Selected route speeds and booth/lane geometry supply the kinematic footprint calculation.
The base network and risk curve are re-evaluated across traffic-flow scenarios.

Base booth types and routes are modified for autonomous demand and a 3:1:1 technology mix.
Base acceleration length and area formulas are recalculated under technology scenarios.
The lane-count rule consumes the New Jersey average and peak flow.
The risk-flow topology supplies the New Jersey merging pattern.
The kinematic geometry supplies fan length, angle, and area for the case.

verification.summary: The summary was reconciled against the body model order and all headline lane, flow, risk, area, autonomy, booth-mix, and case claims.
The introduction was read paragraph by paragraph from public-road motivation through literature branches, synthesis gap, and four work packages.
The symbol table and overall flow chart were checked as interfaces, not treated as decorative front matter.
Equations (1)-(2) were reconciled with their factors, units, citations, and downstream lane-sizing roles.
The focused formula proxy confirms Equations (3)-(7), including K-i in Equation (3), N-i in Equation (5), and the duplicated stay label.
Equation (8), Table 2, and the incorrect prose reference to Equation (6) for queue length were retained exactly.
Equations (9)-(12) and Table 3 were checked for the demand-to-lane chain and the unexplained 4578 veh/h value.
Figure 3 was read as a discrete lane response with no visible numeric sensitivity ledger.
Equations (13)-(20) were reconciled for objective signs, risk coefficients, capacity symbols, and node-balance orientation.
The focused flow-model proxy confirms Equation (21) contains two balance blocks and Equation (22) defines f_i rather than d_i.
Every forward/reverse labeling and augmentation step was retained through the no-augmenting-path termination.
Table 4, the full Figure 4 topology, all Table 5 paths, grouped flows, and 0.96 percent rate were reconciled.
The focused cost proxy confirms Equations (23)-(25), including the printed max objective, a_i>0, weights, and ambiguous speed/deceleration notation.
Figure 6 dimensions reproduce the stated base area only under an implicit geometric formula that the paper does not display.
Every Table 6 traffic/risk cell was retained; the sequence is visibly nonmonotone despite the prose's increasing claim.
Table 7 route totals, unchanged 0.96 percent rate, and Figure 9's 62.25 m label were checked together.
Table 8 and Figure 10 confirm the 3:1:1 mix and 57.31 m acceleration length.
Table 9, Figure 11, Table 10, and Figure 12 were checked for site inputs, daily-flow claims, output units, and 9614.5/9614.56 precision.
Figure 13 supports only a visible comparison direction because its source data cells and uncertainty are absent.
The matrix crop confirms Annex 3 is a capacity adjacency matrix even though its title repeats the delay service-level caption.
LINGO1 was compared line by line with the body risk equation and found to omit the constant, change denominators, minimize an f-independent sum, and bound f by u.
The MATLAB vectors were retained as printed, including mixed /3.6 treatment and Q=max(P), without claiming they reproduce every body length.

results_trace.summary: The baseline lane calculation reports seven one-way toll lanes for four one-way main lanes.
The lane-sensitivity plot reports a positive, discrete relationship between hourly demand and toll-lane count.
The maximum-flow merge example uses five toll lanes for 3000 veh/h.
Five displayed paths are grouped into 1375, 976, and 649 veh/h, summing to 3000 veh/h.
The reported aggregate accident rate for the base merge pattern is 0.96 percent.
The source interprets separated confluence paths as reducing intersections and congestion under the studied flow.
The kinematic calculation reports symmetric acceleration and deceleration lengths of 65.25 m.
The base geometry reports plaza area 4650.1875 m2.
Table 6 risk values remain around 0.91-0.963 percent across the tested demand range.
The maximum-flow curve plateaus at 3000 veh/h when demand exceeds the stated capacity.
Adding 500 autonomous vehicles shifts route-group flows to 1476, 1065, and 826 veh/h.
The autonomy scenario still reports total accident rate 0.96 percent.
A 3:1:1 booth mix reduces the printed acceleration length from 65.25 to 57.31 m.
The source interprets a larger automatic-booth share as reducing area and booth count while increasing capacity.
The New Jersey chart is interpreted as peaking around 07:00 and averaging 2634 veh/h.
The application reports ten toll lanes with a 5:3:2 booth mix.
The application reports 9614.5 m2 area with a 44.8 degree, 131 m fan geometry.
The comparison figure is interpreted as fewer total toll lanes, more automatic lanes, and smaller total footprint than the existing scheme.
The authority letter restates the ten-lane, 5:3:2, 61.28 m, and 9614.5 output as a conditional case rather than a universal design.

contributions.summary: The summary previews lane sizing, risk-flow routing, kinematic area, scenario tests, a site case, and an authority deliverable in execution order.
The introduction moves from transport importance to the toll-plaza bottleneck mechanism before reviewing capacity and safety literature.
The literature gap is framed as missing synthesis across traffic, accident, and cost effects rather than claiming no prior work.
The work map assigns toll-lane number, merge pattern, cost geometry, and scenario stability to distinct analytical jobs.
The overall analysis restates each model as a decision tension with a typed input and output.
Assumptions are paired with justifications and followed by a notation/workflow interface.
Demand and capacity are separated before a multi-channel queue model chooses lane count.
Queue length and delay are translated into qualitative service bands and a numeric intensity lookup.
The algebraic four-step lane algorithm makes the lookup path inspectable before reporting seven lanes.
A graph abstraction converts geometric merging into explicit vertices, arcs, capacities, routes, and objectives.
Throughput and risk are first stated separately before being combined, preserving the trade-off logic.
The labeling algorithm provides a constructive mechanism from formulation to a maximum-flow route.
The full route table connects booth technology, network topology, flow groups, and a safety claim.
The geometry model grounds footprint in braking and following distances rather than an arbitrary taper length.
Three scenario branches distinguish demand, autonomous vehicles, and booth-technology composition.
The site application collects inputs before relaxing assumptions and comparing a candidate with the existing scheme.
The conclusion mirrors the model order and hands explicit limitations to strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
The authority letter translates the technical chain into decision language and closes with an actual-need caveat.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A complete model-and-result preview may reduce coverage-check cost for a judge; this is class-J hypothesis, not scoring evidence.
Separating throughput and risk before combining them may make the trade-off easier to audit; this remains class-J hypothesis.
A route table paired with a network diagram may improve traceability; it is not observed judge preference.
An authority letter may strengthen task closure by translating models into actions; it is not empirical scoring evidence.

weaknesses.summary: Equation (3) uses exponent K-i while Equation (5) uses N-i in otherwise parallel queue factors; K is not separately defined there.
The prose says queue length L_q is calculated by Equation (6), but Equation (5) is the queue-length formula and Equation (6) is expectation additivity.
Normal service/departure distributions do not by themselves justify M/G/K moments, independence, or variance addition, and no sample test is provided.
AADT=38594 with K=0.12 and D=0.60 gives about 2778.8 veh/h, not the printed 4578 veh/h.
Equation (21) includes both a source/sink/intermediate balance and a second balance equal to d_i, while Equation (22) defines f_i instead of d_i.
The network model alternates M_ij and c_ij as capacity concepts without a mapping and gives no lambda value or unit reconciliation.
Equation (23) does not show a km/h-to-m/s conversion although the surrounding speeds are commonly reported in km/h.
Equation (24) has ambiguous powers and braking-deceleration signs, so the printed source and normalized reading require a unit-tested reconstruction.
Model III is named minimum cost and the prose asks to minimize footprint, but Equation (25) displays max Z.
Equation (25) declares a_i>0 while using acceleration and braking deceleration without a complete sign/domain convention; lambda weights are undefined.
Table 6 accident rates are nonmonotone, contradicting the statement that collision rate increases with every flow increase.
Base and autonomous tables both report 0.96 percent total accident rate, inconsistent with the summary's claim of a 0.83 percent reduction.
The New Jersey source, date, facility identity, raw daily profile, 14 m width meaning, and 9614.5/9614.56 precision are not documented.
Annex 3 is titled as delay-based service-level classification but visibly contains a sparse capacity adjacency matrix.
LINGO1 omits +2.7091 and uses C/263 and C/236 instead of the body H_ij/M_ij risk curve.
LINGO1 minimizes sum(u), which is independent of flow f, and bounds f by u rather than capacity c, so it does not implement the printed risk-flow program.
